clinicalPearls: Presents as generalised, symmetrical fine adherent scaling resembling ichthyosis vulgaris but with onset in adolescence or adulthood and no family history.
Extensor surfaces of the limbs and the trunk are typically involved while the flexures are spared; scales are fine and white to brown with a rhomboidal fish-scale pattern.
The classic paraneoplastic association is Hodgkin lymphoma; non-Hodgkin lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, multiple myeloma and some solid tumours (breast, lung) are also reported.
Numerous non-malignant causes must be excluded, including sarcoidosis, HIV, leprosy, hypothyroidism, chronic renal failure, malnutrition and drugs (nicotinic acid, statins, cimetidine, clofazimine).
When paraneoplastic, the ichthyosis tends to parallel tumour activity and may improve with successful treatment of the underlying lymphoma.
Palmoplantar keratoderma and keratosis pilaris-like follicular changes may accompany the scaling.
New-onset ichthyosis in an adult warrants exclusion of lymphoma, particularly with lymphadenopathy, night sweats or weight loss.
reference.pathophysiology: Acquired ichthyosis results from disordered keratinocyte differentiation and desquamation producing retention hyperkeratosis. In lymphoproliferative disease, cytokine-driven alterations in epidermal lipid synthesis and stratum corneum cohesion are implicated, and disturbances of vitamin A and essential fatty acid metabolism have been proposed. Reduced or absent keratohyalin (granular layer) with compact orthohyperkeratosis mirrors the histology of inherited ichthyosis vulgaris. In non-malignant cases, systemic disease, drugs or nutritional deficiency similarly impair normal corneocyte shedding, yielding clinically indistinguishable scaling.
additionalDifferentials: Inherited ichthyosis vulgaris (childhood onset, positive family history)
Nutritional deficiency (essential fatty acids, vitamin A)
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing compact hyperkeratosis with a reduced or absent granular layer
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis with lymph node assessment for lymphoma
Excisional lymph node biopsy where lymphadenopathy is present
Full blood count, ESR and LDH
redFlags: New generalised ichthyosis in an adult without a family history
Associated lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or B symptoms
Rapidly progressive scaling with weight loss
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; when associated with Hodgkin lymphoma the skin often improves with effective chemotherapy and outcome follows that of the treated malignancy.
pitfalls: Dismissing adult-onset scaling as simple xerosis
Failing to distinguish acquired from inherited ichthyosis by age of onset and family history
Overlooking non-malignant causes such as HIV, sarcoidosis and drugs
Not re-evaluating for lymphoma when the scaling recurs
